mainTopic: A dying person's admission of a debt: when it is paid, when orphans are believed, and why it needs no formal witnesses; then a new משנה on collecting written versus oral loans
overview: This amud continues the discussion of a dying person (שכיב מרע) who admits he owes money. The גמרא asks why רב הונא pays the debt from property given to הקדש, when רב ושמואל worry that people pretend to owe money so they won't look rich. After one answer fails, רב נחמן explains that both cases involve a שטר. In רב הונא's case the court already confirmed it. In רב ושמואל's case it was not confirmed, and saying "תנו" counts as the dying man confirming it. Next, רבה rules on orphans who claim the debt was already paid. After an objection, the גמרא restates his ruling: the orphans are believed if their father said "מנה לפלוני בידי" and later said he paid, but not if he had said "תנו". Then רבא asks whether a dying man's admission needs "אתם עדי" or "כתובו", and he answers that a person does not joke at the time of death, so his words are like a written, delivered document. Finally, a new משנה teaches that a loan with a שטר is collected even from sold property, while a loan before עדים only is collected only from property the borrower still owns.

steps.title: Why not apply the 'not looking rich' worry to the הקדש case too?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב הונא with the reasoning of רב ושמואל: a person may falsely claim debts so he won't seem wealthy.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too, in רב הונא's case of הקדש, we should say: a person tends to say things so that he won't look rich!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב הונא's ruling. It takes the reason רב ושמואל gave and asks why that reason doesn't apply to the dying man who gave everything to הקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ושמואל said a dying man's 'I owe money' might not be true, because people pretend to owe money so they don't seem wealthy. If so, the dying man in רב הונא's case might also be making up the debt. Then we would be taking money away from הקדש for no real reason.

keyTerms.meaning: Here too, applying the same logic to this case
A person tends to / is likely to
To make himself look 'full' (wealthy)
Property given to the Temple treasury

phrases.english: Here too,
phrases.notes: 'Here' means רב הונא's case, where the dying man gave all his property to הקדש.

phrases.english: a person is prone
not to make himself appear sated!
phrases.notes: He means not wanting to look rich, so he might claim debts he doesn't really owe.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכָא נָמֵי, אָדָם עָשׂוּי שֶׁלֹּא לְהַשְׂבִּיעַ אֶת עַצְמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the reasoning of רב ושמואל (stated just before this section) against רב הונא's ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's ruling that a dying man who gave everything to הקדש is believed when he admits a debt
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If people commonly make up debts so they won't look rich, the admission in the הקדש case should also be doubted.

steps.title: רב הונא is talking about a creditor who holds a document
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא's ruling applies only when the creditor has a שטר that backs up the dying man's admission.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב הונא said there that we pay, he meant a case where the creditor is holding a שטר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing רב הונא's case: the creditor has a written loan document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a שטר in hand, the debt doesn't rest only on the dying man's words, so the worry that he made it up falls away. רב ושמואל's worry stays true in general. It just doesn't apply when there is written proof.

keyTerms.meaning: When he said it, this is the case he meant
Holds
A written document, here a loan document

phrases.english: When Rav Huna said there
it was where he holds a document.
phrases.notes: 'He' is the creditor the dying man said he owed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 1 by limiting רב הונא's case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב הונא's ruling seemed to rely only on the dying man's word, which is open to the 'not looking rich' worry.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב הונא's case has a שטר, so the debt is backed by proof.

steps.title: Then רב ושמואל must mean an oral loan, which they say can't be collected from heirs
steps.stepSummary: If רב הונא means a case with a שטר, then רב ושמואל must mean a case without one. But רב ושמואל themselves hold that a מלוה על פה is not collected from heirs, so how could saying "תנו" help?
steps.simpleTranslation: It follows that רב ושמואל are talking about a creditor with no שטר. But then how can it be that if he said "Give," the heirs give? It is a מלוה על פה, and רב ושמואל both say that an oral loan cannot be collected from heirs or from buyers!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a conclusion from the last answer, and that conclusion creates a contradiction within רב ושמואל's own views.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the difference between the two rulings is having a שטר or not, then רב ושמואל's case has no document, which makes it a מלוה על פה. Yet רב ושמואל hold that a מלוה על פה cannot be collected from יורשין. So their ruling that the heirs pay after "תנו" would clash with their own rule.

keyTerms.meaning: By inference / it follows that
'Give!', the dying man's instruction to pay
An oral loan, with no written document
Heirs
Buyers of the debtor's land

steps.confusionAlert: The challenge is not that רב ושמואל contradict רב הונא. The problem is that the proposed answer makes רב ושמואל contradict their own other ruling about מלוה על פה.

phrases.english: By inference, that of Rav and Shmuel
is where he does not hold a document;
he said "Give" — they give?!
phrases.notes: 'They give' means the money is paid out of what the heirs received.

phrases.english: It is an oral loan,
and Rav and Shmuel both say:
An oral loan — one does not collect

phrases.aramaic: לֹא מִן הַיּוֹרְשִׁין וְלֹא מִן הַלָּקוֹחוֹת!
phrases.english: neither from the heirs nor from the purchasers!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִכְּלָל דְּרַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל דְּלָא נָקֵיט שְׁטָרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a conclusion from step 2's answer and shows it leads to a contradiction.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer of step 2, which separates the cases by having a שטר or not
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Without a שטר, רב ושמואל's case is a מלוה על פה, and by their own rule it could not be collected from the heirs even if he said "תנו".

steps.title: רב נחמן: both cases have a document; the difference is whether it was confirmed
steps.stepSummary: Both rulings involve a שטר. In רב הונא's case the שטר was already confirmed by the court (מקויים). In רב ושמואל's case it was not, and the dying man's "תנו" serves as his confirmation of the document.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב נחמן said: in both cases the creditor holds a שטר, and there is no contradiction. רב הונא's case is where the שטר was confirmed. רב ושמואל's case is where it was not confirmed. If the dying man said "Give," he confirmed the שטר. If he did not say "Give," he did not confirm it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן drops the earlier answer and offers a new way to tell the two rulings apart: whether the שטר was confirmed by the court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since both cases have a שטר, neither is a מלוה על פה, so the problem from step 3 disappears. A שטר that has not been confirmed isn't enough on its own. When the dying man says "תנו," he is admitting the שטר is real, which confirms it. If he doesn't say it, the 'not looking rich' worry means his words don't confirm the שטר.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, rejecting the earlier answer for a new one
Both this and that
And it is not difficult; the two cases differ
Confirmed (ratified) by the court as a genuine document
He confirmed his document

steps.whatToRemember: Final picture: a dying man's admission of a debt is paid when it is backed by a שטר. If the court already confirmed the שטר, it is paid even from property given to הקדש (רב הונא). If the שטר was not confirmed, it is paid only if he said "תנו," which counts as confirming it (רב ושמואל).
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that a dying man's spoken words can do the job of court confirmation for a שטר, but only when he clearly tells them to pay.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Nachman said:
Both this and that are where he holds a document,
and it is not difficult:
this is where it is ratified,
phrases.notes: 'This' is רב הונא's case: the court has already confirmed the document is genuine.

phrases.english: that is where it is not ratified;
he said "Give" — he ratified his document,
he did not say "Give" — he did not ratify his document.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: אִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי דְּנָקֵיט שְׁטָרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects step 2's answer because of step 3's challenge, and gives a new answer to step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New distinction between the cases: a confirmed שטר versus an unconfirmed שטר
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The difference seemed to be a שטר versus no שטר, which turned רב ושמואל's case into a מלוה על פה.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both cases have a שטר. רב הונא's is confirmed. In רב ושמואל's, saying "תנו" is what confirms it.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The rulings agree once we see that "תנו" works as the dying man's confirmation of an unconfirmed שטר.

steps.title: רבה's ruling on orphans who claim they repaid
steps.stepSummary: רבה rules on a שכיב מרע who admitted a debt. If he said 'מנה לפלוני בידי' and the orphans say 'we paid', they are believed. If he said 'תנו מנה לפלוני' and they say 'we paid', they are not believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: A dying man said, 'So-and-so has a מנה in my hand,' and the orphans later said, 'We paid it.' They are believed. If he said, 'Give a מנה to so-and-so,' and the orphans said, 'We paid it,' they are not believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new ruling from רבה. It compares two ways a dying man can admit a debt and asks whether his orphans are believed when they say they already paid it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two kinds of wording. 'מנה לפלוני בידי' is a plain statement of fact. 'תנו מנה לפלוני' is a direct order to pay. רבה says the orphans' claim of payment works with the first wording but not with the second.

keyTerms.meaning: A person who is seriously ill and may die
A sum of money (100 זוז)
In my hand, meaning I hold money that belongs to him
Orphans, here the heirs
They are believed

phrases.english: Rabba said:
A dangerously ill person who said
"So-and-so has a maneh in my hand,"
phrases.notes: A maneh is a sum of money worth 100 zuz. He is saying he owes this person that amount.

phrases.english: and the orphans said "We repaid it"
they are believed.
"Give a maneh to so-and-so,"
and the orphans said "We repaid it"
they are not believed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic. Like the earlier steps, it deals with the deathbed wording 'תנו', but now the question is the orphans' claim that the debt was paid.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Orphans who say they paid are believed when the father said 'מנה לפלוני בידי'. They are not believed when he said 'תנו מנה לפלוני'.

steps.title: The גמרא says the logic should be reversed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that רבה's ruling seems backwards. A firm order like 'תנו' would push the orphans to pay right away, so their claim of payment should be more believable there, not less.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which way is this going? The opposite makes more sense! If he said 'Give a מנה', their father settled the matter firmly, so it is likely they paid. If he said 'So-and-so has a מנה in my hand', their father did not settle the matter firmly, so it is likely they did not pay!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבה's ruling and says the opposite makes more sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With 'תנו', the father gave a clear order, so the orphans would rush to carry it out. That makes 'we paid' believable. With 'מנה לפלוני בידי', there was no order, so they had less reason to pay quickly. That makes 'we paid' less believable. This is exactly the reverse of what רבה said.

keyTerms.meaning: Which way is this going? (an expression that something sounds upside down)
The opposite makes more sense
He settled the matter firmly
They paid him

phrases.english: Which way is this going?
phrases.notes: This is a way of saying 'this sounds upside down.'

phrases.english: The opposite makes more sense!
If he said "Give a maneh"
since their father stated the matter firmly,
one can say that they paid him.
If he said "So-and-so has a maneh in my hand"
since their father did not state the matter firmly,
one can say that they did not pay him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling of רבה in step 5.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A firm order ('תנו') makes payment more likely, so the orphans should be believed there. A plain statement makes payment less likely. רבה's ruling is the reverse.

steps.title: רבה's ruling restated: the father later said he paid
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא restates רבה's ruling. The orphans are not saying 'we paid'. They are saying 'father later told us he had paid.' After 'מנה לפלוני בידי' they are believed, since he may have just remembered. After 'תנו' they are not believed, since he would not have given that order if he had already paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, if it was said, this is how it was said: A dying man said, 'So-and-so has a מנה in my hand,' and the orphans said, 'Father later told us: I paid.' They are believed. Why? He remembered. If he said, 'Give a מנה to so-and-so,' and the orphans said, 'Father later said: I paid,' they are not believed. If he had really paid, he would not have said 'Give.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the objection by restating what רבה actually said. The orphans' claim is about what their father told them later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the question is whether the father could change his own statement. A plain statement like 'מנה לפלוני בידי' can be honestly mistaken, so a later 'I paid' makes sense. He simply remembered. A firm order like 'תנו' shows he was sure he owed the money, so a later 'I paid' is not believed.

keyTerms.meaning: If it was said, this is how it was said (the גמרא restating a ruling)
He later said (taking back what he said before)
I paid
He remembered

steps.whatToRemember: A plain statement of a debt ('מנה לפלוני בידי') can be corrected later, since the father may have just remembered. A firm order to pay ('תנו') cannot be corrected by a later 'I paid.'
steps.confusionAlert: The restated version is not about the orphans paying. It is about the father himself later saying he had paid.

phrases.english: Rather, if it was said, this is how it was said:
A dangerously ill person who said
"So-and-so has a maneh in my hand,"
and the orphans said:
"Father later told us: I paid it"
they are believed.
What is the reason? He remembered.
phrases.notes: At first he forgot that he had paid. Later it came back to him.

phrases.english: If he said "Give a maneh to so-and-so,"
and the orphans said:
"Father later said: I paid it"
they are not believed.
For if it were true that he had paid him,
he would not have said "Give."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of step 6 by restating the case behind רבה's ruling from step 5.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבה was talking about the orphans claiming that they themselves paid, and then his ruling looks backwards.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבה was talking about the orphans claiming their father later said he paid. That claim is believed after a plain statement ('בידי'), since he may have remembered. It is not believed after a firm order ('תנו').

steps.title: רבא asks whether a deathbed admission needs witnesses or writing
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks whether a שכיב מרע who admits a debt must say 'אתם עדי' or 'כתובו' for it to count. The question depends on whether a person jokes at the time of death.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked: A dying man who admitted a debt, what is the law? Must he say 'You are my witnesses,' or does he not need to? Must he say 'Write it down,' or does he not need to? Does a person joke at the time of death, or does a person not joke at the time of death?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא raises a new question about a dying man's admission. He asks whether it needs the usual formal steps to be binding.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally an admission only counts if the person says 'אתם עדי' (and saying 'כתובו' lets a document be written). Otherwise he may have been joking. רבא asks whether a dying person is assumed to be serious, so these steps are not needed.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked (raised a question to be worked out; the next step answers it)
He admitted (that he owed money)
You are my witnesses
Write it down
Joking, not speaking seriously

steps.confusionAlert: רבא here is a different אמורא from רבה in step 5. The names look alike but are two different people.
steps.whyThisMatters: The whole question comes down to one idea: is a dying person assumed to speak seriously?

phrases.english: Rava asked:
A dangerously ill person who admitted a debt, what is the law?
Must he say "You are my witnesses,"
or does he not need to say "You are my witnesses"?
Must he say "Write it down,"
or does he not need to say "Write it down"?
Does a person joke at the time of death,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ אֵין אָדָם מְשַׁטֶּה בִּשְׁעַת מִיתָה?
phrases.english: or does a person not joke at the time of death?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new question about deathbed admissions after the discussion of רבה's ruling has ended.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a שכיב מרע's admission needs 'אתם עדי' or 'כתובו' to be binding. This depends on whether a person jokes at the time of death.

steps.title: רבא answers his own question: a dying man does not joke
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that אין אדם משטה בשעת מיתה. A שכיב מרע's words are treated as if written and handed over, so his admission counts without 'אתם עדי' or 'כתובו'.
steps.simpleTranslation: After רבא asked the question, he answered it himself. A person does not joke when he is about to die. So the words of a שכיב מרע are treated as if they were written down and handed over.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the question he asked in Step 8. A dying man's admission counts even without the formal words 'אתם עדי' or 'כתובו'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question in Step 8 was whether we worry that a dying man might be joking. רבא decides that we do not, because nobody jokes at the time of death. So his plain words carry the full weight of a written and delivered document.

keyTerms.meaning: He resolved it, he answered the question
Jokes, says something without meaning it
At the time of death
As if written and handed over, the full legal force of a delivered document

steps.whatToRemember: A שכיב מרע's spoken words count like a written, delivered document, because a person does not joke when he is about to die.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the halacha that a שכיב מרע's admission of a debt is binding even without formal witness language. It closes the sugya about deathbed admissions.

phrases.english: After he asked it, he then resolved it:
A person does not joke at the time of death,
and the words of a person on his deathbed
are like written and handed-over words.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question רבא raised in Step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a שכיב מרע must say 'אתם עדי' or 'כתובו' for his admission of a debt to count.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No. A person does not joke at the time of death, so a שכיב מרע's words are like a written and delivered document.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: דברי שכיב מרע ככתובין וכמסורין דמו. His admission is binding without formal words.

steps.title: New משנה: a loan with a document versus a loan before witnesses
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a loan made with a שטר can be collected from נכסים משועבדים. A loan made only in front of עדים can be collected only from נכסים בני חורין.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Someone who lends money to another person with a שטר can collect from property that was mortgaged to the loan, even after it was sold. Someone who lends in front of עדים only can collect only from property the borrower still owns.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with a new topic. It contrasts two kinds of loans and the property each lender may collect from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A loan with a שטר creates a lien on the borrower's land. So the lender can collect it even from buyers who bought that land after the loan. A loan made with only עדים lets the lender collect only from land the borrower still owns, not from land he already sold.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מַתְנִיתִין, our משנה
A written loan document
Mortgaged property, land the borrower sold to others after taking the loan
Witnesses, here a loan witnessed but not written down
Free property, land the borrower still owns

steps.confusionAlert: 'בני חורין' here does not mean free people. It means 'free' property, land with no buyer's claim on it because the borrower still owns it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This משנה is the basic source for the difference in collection rights between a written loan and an oral loan. That difference runs through all of דיני ממונות.

phrases.english: MISHNAH: One who lends to his fellow with a document
collects from mortgaged property.
phrases.notes: This is land the borrower sold after the loan. The lender may take it from the buyer.

phrases.english: With witnesses only,
they collect from free property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה with a new topic. It does not continue the deathbed-admission discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A loan with a שטר is collected even from נכסים משועבדים. A loan with only עדים is collected only from נכסים בני חורין.
